title: Ten-Letter Gene Repeats
statement:
A DNA strand is a string s made of the letters A, C, G and T. Return every substring of length exactly 10 that occurs more than once in s. Occurrences may overlap.

List each such substring once, in any order.

examples.why: The strand repeats every 4 letters, so each 10-letter window equals the one 4 places later. The window starting at index 3 has no partner, because index 7 would run past the end.
The two windows overlap in nine letters, and that still counts. The answer lists the repeat once.

constraints: s[i] is one of A, C, G, T
hints: Slide a window of length 10 across the string. How do you know whether you have seen the current window before?
Keep two sets: windows seen once, and windows already reported. That reports each repeat exactly once.
To skip building strings, encode each letter in 2 bits. A 10-letter window is then a 20-bit number you can update in O(1) as the window slides.

explain.intuition:
There are only n − 9 windows of length 10. Put each one in a set; if it is already there, it is a repeat. A second set (or a count map) makes sure a window that appears three times is reported once.

Slicing a 10-character string for every window is fine here, but there is a neat upgrade: with four letters, each fits in 2 bits, so a whole window fits in a 20-bit integer. Sliding the window is a shift left by 2, an OR with the new letter, and a mask to drop the oldest letter. It is the same idea as a rolling hash, with no collisions.
steps: If s is shorter than 11, return an empty list.
For each start i from 0 to n − 10, take the window s[i..i+9].
If the window is in seen, add it to repeated; otherwise add it to seen.
pitfalls: Adding a window to the answer each time it is seen again, which lists a triple repeat twice.
Stepping by 10 instead of 1, which skips overlapping windows like in the second example.
Off-by-one on the last window: the last start is n − 10, not n − 11.

complexity.time: O(n) with the bit encoding, O(10·n) with slices

solutions.title: Compare every pair of windows
solutions.idea: For each window, look for an equal window at any later start.

solutions.title: Two sets of window strings
solutions.idea: Remember every window. The second time one shows up, put it in the answer set.

solutions.title: 2-bit rolling code
solutions.idea: Encode each letter in 2 bits. The window is a 20-bit number updated with a shift, an OR and a mask, and counted in a typed array.

followups: The window length L is now a parameter up to 100 000. Why does slicing become too slow, and how does a polynomial rolling hash fix it?
Return the repeats in order of their first occurrence.
